topic: SAT Writing: commas and run-on sentences
why_it_matters: The same few comma rules come up again and again on the SAT, and in every college essay or job email someone reads to decide about you.

concepts.text: Two complete sentences can be joined only with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS word (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so)
A comma alone can't join two complete sentences; that mistake is called a comma splice
Commas go where the sentence's structure needs them, not wherever you pause when you read it aloud

misconception: You put a comma wherever you pause, so 'I was tired, I went to bed' is a fine sentence
root_prerequisite: Telling a complete sentence (subject + verb + complete thought) from a fragment

boss.name: Pause-Pause Penguin
boss.backstory: A penguin in a giant comma necklace, holding a sign that reads "I PAUSED, SO COMMA".

cliffhanger: I heard a colon can only come after a complete sentence. Even before a list. That can't be right… right?

quiz.question: Join 'The bus was late' and 'we missed the first bell' into one correct sentence.
quiz.answer: The bus was late, so we missed the first bell. (Also correct: The bus was late; we missed the first bell.)

quiz.question: Is this sentence correct: 'My phone died, I couldn't call you.' Why or why not?
quiz.answer: No. It is a comma splice: two complete sentences joined by only a comma. Fix it with a period, a semicolon, or ', so'.

quiz.question: Does 'The tallest girl on the team scored twice' need a comma after 'team'?
quiz.answer: No. 'The tallest girl on the team' is who did it and 'scored' is what she did; a single comma never goes between them, even if you pause there.
